questions.question: In May 2025, the Supreme Court set aside which High Court order that had denied maternity leave to a government school teacher for the birth of their third child?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Madras High Court**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__
 __ 
• In **May 2025**, the **Supreme Court of India** set aside an order passed by the **Madras High Court** that had denied maternity leave to a government school teacher for the birth of her third child. 
• The teacher had previously been denied maternity leave citing the **two-child policy**, which is a guideline followed in some government sectors to limit benefits to employees with only two children. 
• The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the teacher, emphasizing the importance of **maternity rights** and the welfare of children irrespective of birth order. 
• The judgment reaffirmed the principles of **gender equality** and **women's rights** guaranteed under the **Indian Constitution**, including **Article 42**, which directs the state to make provisions for securing just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. 
• This decision has significant implications for **maternity leave policies** and reinforces the need to balance population control policies with the fundamental rights of individuals. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Madras High Court:** 
• The **Madras High Court** is one of the oldest High Courts in India, established in **1862**, and it has jurisdiction over the state of Tamil Nadu and the Union Territory of Puducherry. 
• It has been involved in several landmark cases, shaping the interpretation of laws and constitutional provisions in India. 
• **Maternity Benefits in India:** 
• The **Maternity Benefit Act, 1961**, as amended in **2017**, provides women with **26 weeks** of paid maternity leave for the first two children and **12 weeks** for subsequent children. 
• It applies to all establishments employing **10 or more workers**, aiming to ensure the health and well-being of both the mother and child. 
• **Supreme Court's Role in Protecting Women's Rights:** 
• The **Supreme Court of India** has consistently upheld women's rights, including maternity leave, as part of the fundamental rights under **Articles 14, 15, and 21** of the Constitution. 
• In past rulings, the Court has highlighted the need for a supportive work environment for women to balance their professional and personal responsibilities. 
• **Two-Child Policy:** 
• Some government policies in India, particularly in the past, have implemented a **two-child norm** to control population growth. 
• This norm has been criticized for being discriminatory and violating fundamental rights, especially when linked to eligibility for government benefits or employment. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Significance of Maternity Leave:** 
• Maternity leave is essential to ensure the health and well-being of the mother and child during and after pregnancy. 
• It also promotes **gender equality** in the workplace and encourages women’s participation in the workforce. 
• **Role of Judiciary:** 
• The judiciary plays a crucial role in interpreting and enforcing laws to protect women's rights, including maternity benefits. 
• Judgments such as this one set precedents that influence policies and promote social justice.

questions.question: As of December 2024, ______ million women in India were monitoring their credit, signalling growing financial awareness.
questions.solution:

 __ 
• As of **December 2024**, approximately **27 million women in India** were actively monitoring their credit. This indicates a significant rise in **financial literacy** and awareness among women in the country. 
• This data reflects the growing participation of women in managing personal finances, which marks a transformative shift in **financial inclusion** and empowerment. 
• Credit monitoring is crucial for individuals to understand their financial health and maintain a good **credit score**, which directly impacts loan approvals and interest rates. 
• The number **27 million** signifies an increasing trend among women to take control of their financial decisions, enabled by initiatives promoting **financial literacy**. 
• This growth can be attributed to various governmental and non-governmental programs encouraging women to adopt **financial tools** like credit monitoring and budgeting. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Importance of Credit Monitoring:** 
• Credit monitoring allows individuals to track their **credit history** and **credit score**, which are critical for securing loans, credit cards, and mortgages. 
• It helps detect **fraudulent activities** or errors in the credit report, ensuring financial security. 
• Regular credit monitoring can improve financial planning by providing insights into spending patterns and debt management. 
• **Financial Inclusion in India:** 
• **Financial inclusion** refers to providing affordable financial services to underprivileged and low-income groups, including women. 
• Government schemes like **Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY)** have played a significant role in increasing access to financial products and services. 
• **Role of Technology:** 
• The rise in credit monitoring among women is facilitated by the availability of **digital platforms** and **mobile apps**. 
• Technological advancements have made financial tools more accessible and user-friendly for individuals, contributing to increased participation. 
• **Government and NGO Initiatives:** 
• Programs like **Financial Literacy Camps** conducted by banks and NGOs aim to educate women about financial management and credit awareness. 
• Collaborations between private organizations and the government have further enhanced financial education efforts. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Gender Gap in Financial Literacy:** 
• Historically, there has been a significant **gender gap** in financial literacy, with women being less likely than men to access financial services or monitor their credit. 
• Efforts to close this gap are crucial for achieving **gender equality** in financial empowerment. 
• **Credit Score and Its Implications:** 
• A **credit score** is a numerical representation of an individual’s creditworthiness, ranging from 300 to 900. 
• Higher scores indicate better financial health and improve the chances of securing loans with favorable terms. 
• **Global Comparisons:** 
• India's progress in financial inclusion among women is notable, but there is still room for improvement compared to developed countries where **financial literacy** rates are higher. 
• Global initiatives like the **World Bank’s Financial Inclusion Support Framework** are instrumental in driving such progress worldwide.

questions.solution:

 __ 
• **Hesaraghatta Grasslands** are located near **Bengaluru**, the capital city of **Karnataka**, India. 
• These grasslands are an **ecologically sensitive area** and serve as an essential habitat for various species of flora and fauna. 
• The region is known for its **open grassland ecosystem**, which is rare in the area and is crucial for biodiversity conservation. 
• Hesaraghatta is also home to the **Hesaraghatta Lake**, a man-made reservoir built in **1894** to supply water to Bengaluru. 
• It is a popular destination for **bird watchers**, as the grasslands attract numerous species of migratory and resident birds. 
• Threats such as urbanization and encroachment have raised concerns about the **protection of the grasslands** and its biodiversity. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Location and Geography:** 
• Hesaraghatta Grasslands are situated approximately **30 km northwest** of Bengaluru city, Karnataka. 
• The area covers **hundreds of acres** and includes both grasslands and a freshwater lake. 
• The grasslands are part of the **semi-arid ecosystem** typical of the Deccan Plateau region. 
• **Biodiversity:** 
• The grasslands support a variety of species, including **mammals, birds, insects, and reptiles**. 
• It is especially famous for attracting bird species like **Black Drongo, Indian Roller, and Brahminy Kite**. 
• The area also has a significant population of **grassland-dependent insects**, which contribute to the ecosystem's health. 
• **Hesaraghatta Lake:** 
• The lake was built in **1894** under the supervision of Sir **M. Visvesvaraya**, a renowned engineer. 
• It was designed to supply drinking water to Bengaluru and is fed by the **Arkavathy River**. 
• Over the years, the lake has dried up due to **declining water levels** and silt deposition. 
• **Conservation Concerns:** 
• Rapid **urbanization** and illegal encroachments pose significant threats to the grasslands. 
• Environmental activists have called for the **protection and restoration** of the area to prevent biodiversity loss. 
• The Karnataka government has proposed **ecotourism initiatives**, but these have been met with concerns about potential ecological damage. 
• **Importance of Grasslands:** 
• Grasslands play a crucial role in **carbon sequestration**, helping to combat climate change. 
• They are vital for sustaining **livestock grazing** and supporting rural livelihoods. 
• Grasslands act as a natural **water recharge zone**, contributing to groundwater replenishment. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Hesaraghatta Grasslands:** 
• The grasslands have been a focal point of conservation debates in Karnataka due to their ecological significance. 
• Efforts are being made to prevent the conversion of grasslands into urban or industrial areas. 
• Local communities often depend on the grasslands for **agriculture and livestock grazing**. 
• **Biodiversity Significance:** 
• Grasslands like Hesaraghatta are crucial for migratory bird species and act as stopovers during seasonal movements. 
• They provide habitat for endemic species that are not found in other ecosystems. 
• **Conservation Efforts:** 
• NGOs and environmental activists are advocating for legal protection under wildlife conservation laws. 
• Public awareness campaigns highlight the importance of preserving such ecosystems to avoid irreversible damage. </ul

questions.question: Which among the following is a wind instrument?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pava**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pava** is a traditional wind instrument that belongs to the family of musical instruments that produce sound by the vibration of air, typically using a player's breath.
 
• It is commonly used in various folk and classical performances and is known for its melodious and soothing sound.
 
• Unlike percussion instruments like **Dhol** or **Nagara**, which rely on striking a surface, wind instruments like the Pava generate sound through the manipulation of air.
 
• Wind instruments have a long history and are deeply embedded in cultural and musical traditions across the world. The Pava specifically is a part of traditional and cultural Indian music.
 
• Other examples of wind instruments include the flute, clarinet, and shehnai. These instruments often require a great deal of skill and breath control.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Dhol:**

 
 
• **Dhol** is a percussion instrument and not a wind instrument. It is widely used in folk music and celebrations, especially in North India, Punjab, and Pakistan.
 
• It consists of a cylindrical wooden shell covered with animal skin or synthetic material and is played using sticks.
 
• It is integral to Bhangra and other traditional dance forms.
 
 
 
• **Manjira:**
 
 
• **Manjira** is a traditional Indian percussion instrument made of a pair of small metallic cymbals.
 
• It is used to provide rhythmic accompaniment in devotional and folk music.
 
• Manjira is not a wind instrument as it produces sound through the striking of metal surfaces.
 
 
 
• **Nagara:**
 
 
• **Nagara** is a large drum that is also categorized as a percussion instrument.
 
• It is commonly used in religious ceremonies, folk performances, and traditional Indian music.
 
• Sound is generated by striking the drumhead with sticks, which makes it distinct from wind instruments.
 
 
 
• **Wind Instruments:**
 
 
• **Characteristics:** Wind instruments produce sound by the vibration of air inside a tube or body of the instrument.
 
• **Examples:** Flute, clarinet, saxophone, shehnai, and Pava.
 
• **Function:** The player blows air into or across an opening, and different notes are produced by changing the length of the air column inside the instrument.
 
• **Applications:** These instruments are widely used in classical, folk, and modern music across various cultures globally.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Significance:** Wind instruments have been used for centuries in rituals, religious ceremonies, and entertainment, showcasing their cultural importance.
 
• **Scientific Basis:** The sound in wind instruments is produced by the vibration of air columns, which is manipulated by changing the length of the column using finger holes or valves.
 
• **Global Examples:** Instruments like the flute (India), bagpipes (Scotland), and pan pipes (South America) highlight the diversity of wind instruments worldwide.

questions.question: In 2024, which newly discovered "mini-moon" was expected to orbit Earth for about two months?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2024 Roxana**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **2024 Roxana** is a newly discovered "mini-moon" expected to orbit Earth for about two months in **2024**.

• Mini-moons are temporary satellites of Earth, typically small celestial objects that are captured by Earth's gravitational field.

• 2024 Roxana's discovery highlights the ongoing advancements in **astronomical observation** and **tracking technologies**.

• Such mini-moons are scientifically significant as they provide insights into **Earth's gravitational interactions** with space objects and offer opportunities for further space exploration.

• The name "Roxana" was selected following international naming conventions for celestial bodies and reflects the growing catalog of space objects tracked by astronomers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Mini-Moons:**

• Mini-moons are **small asteroids or space rocks** temporarily captured by Earth's gravitational pull.

• They usually orbit Earth for a short duration, ranging from weeks to a few months, before escaping Earth's gravity.

• Their study helps scientists understand **gravitational dynamics** and interactions between Earth and nearby celestial objects.

• **Detection of Mini-Moons:**

• Modern telescopes and tracking systems, such as **Pan-STARRS** and **ATLAS**, play a crucial role in identifying these objects.

• Mini-moons are usually detected when their orbits bring them close to Earth, making them visible through advanced imaging technology.

• **Scientific Importance:**

• Mini-moons serve as potential targets for future **space missions**, including asteroid mining and exploration.

• Studying their composition can provide insights into the **early solar system** and the formation of planets.

• **Notable Mini-Moons:**

• Previous mini-moons include **2006 RH120**, a space rock that orbited Earth briefly in 2006.

• Another example is **2020 CD3**, which orbited Earth for several months before leaving in 2020.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Gravitational Interaction:** Mini-moons are captured by Earth's gravity when their trajectories align with Earth's orbit. These interactions provide valuable data for understanding **orbital mechanics**.

• **Exploration Opportunities:** Mini-moons present unique opportunities for close-range exploration, potentially serving as stepping stones for **deep-space missions**.

• **Global Collaboration:** Discovering and tracking mini-moons often involves **international cooperation** among observatories and space agencies.
</ul

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: Which of the following policies were devised by Lord Dalhousie?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Doctrine of Lapse**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Doctrine of Lapse**: This policy was devised and implemented by **Lord Dalhousie** during his tenure as the Governor-General of India (1848-1856). It allowed the British East India Company to annex Indian princely states if the ruler died without a legitimate male heir. *Hence, this statement is correct.* 
• **Policy of Paramountcy**: Although the concept of paramountcy (British supremacy over Indian states) was strengthened during Lord Dalhousie's tenure, it was initiated earlier by other British officials. Dalhousie expanded its scope but did not devise the policy. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.* 
• **Subsidiary Alliance**: This policy was introduced by **Lord Wellesley** (1798-1805), not Lord Dalhousie. It required Indian rulers to accept British forces in their territories and pay for their maintenance, effectively reducing their sovereignty. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.* 
• **Policy of Non-Intervention**: This policy was followed during the early British rule in India, particularly under Warren Hastings, but was abandoned by later Governor-Generals, including Lord Dalhousie. Dalhousie was known for his interventionist policies. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.* 
• ***Therefore, the correct answer is Doctrine of Lapse.*** 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Doctrine of Lapse:** 
• Introduced by **Lord Dalhousie** as a means to expand British control in India. 
• If a ruler died without a legitimate male heir, the state was annexed by the British East India Company. 
• This policy led to the annexation of several states such as **Satara (1848), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854), and Awadh (1856)**. 
• The doctrine was highly controversial and led to widespread resentment among Indian rulers, contributing to the **1857 Revolt**. 
• **Policy of Paramountcy:** 
• Established British supremacy over Indian princely states. 
• Provided the British with the authority to intervene in the internal affairs of Indian states. 
• Expanded during Dalhousie's tenure but was not originally devised by him. 
• **Subsidiary Alliance:** 
• Introduced by **Lord Wellesley** in the early 19th century. 
• Required Indian rulers to accept British forces and pay for their maintenance. 
• Reduced the sovereignty of Indian states and brought them under British control. 
• **Policy of Non-Intervention:** 
• Followed by early British administrators like Warren Hastings. 
• Aimed at minimizing interference in Indian states' internal affairs. 
• Later abandoned in favor of more interventionist policies. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Impact of the Doctrine of Lapse:** 
• Created distrust and resentment among Indian rulers. 
• Contributed to the growing dissatisfaction that led to the **1857 Revolt**. 
• Highlighted the exploitative nature of British policies in India. 
• **Lord Dalhousie’s Reforms:** 
• Introduced modern infrastructure, including **railways, telegraphs, and postal systems**. 
• Focused on administrative efficiency and centralization. 
• Implemented the **Wood's Dispatch (1854)** for education reform.

questions.question: In which year did the National Stock Exchange began its operations?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1994**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **National Stock Exchange (NSE)** of India began its operations in the year **1994**. It was established to bring transparency and efficiency to the Indian capital markets.
 
• NSE was incorporated in **1992** as a tax-paying company and received recognition as a stock exchange under the **Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956**, in April 1993.
 
• The NSE commenced trading in the wholesale debt market segment in **June 1994**, followed by equity trading in **November 1994**.
 
• It was India's first exchange to offer a fully automated, screen-based electronic trading system, which provided easy accessibility and an efficient trading platform to investors.
 
• NSE has played a critical role in transforming India’s capital markets, enhancing market integrity, and promoting investor confidence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **National Stock Exchange (NSE):**

 
 
• The NSE is headquartered in **Mumbai, Maharashtra**, and is one of the largest and most advanced stock exchanges in India.
 
• The exchange's flagship index, the **NIFTY 50**, is used by investors in India and globally as a barometer of the Indian capital market.
 
• The NSE is regulated by the **Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)**.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of NSE:**
 
 
• It introduced the concept of a **demutualized exchange** in India, separating ownership and management from the trading rights.
 
• NSE was the first exchange in India to offer a **derivatives trading platform**, beginning with the launch of index futures in **2000**.
 
• The exchange provides trading in various financial instruments, including **equities, debt, derivatives, and currency derivatives**.
 
 
 
• **Other Stock Exchanges in India:**
 
 
• The **Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE)** is the oldest stock exchange in Asia, established in **1875**.
 
• While BSE has historical significance, NSE has outpaced it in terms of trading volume and technological advancements.
 
 
 
• **Importance of NSE:**
 
 
• NSE has enhanced **transparency** by introducing electronic trading, reducing fraud and malpractices.
 
• It has made capital markets more **accessible** to retail investors, providing fair pricing mechanisms.
 
• The exchange is instrumental in **mobilizing savings** for economic development by providing a platform for investment in securities.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **SEBI and Market Regulation:**

 
 
• The **Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)** was established in **1988** and given statutory powers in **1992** to regulate the securities market in India.
 
• SEBI plays a key role in protecting the interests of investors and ensuring a fair and transparent trading environment.
 
 
 
• **Technological Advancements:**
 
 
• NSE’s trading platform is based on a state-of-the-art electronic trading system, capable of handling a large number of orders per second.
 
• The exchange provides **real-time price dissemination** to ensure informed decision-making by investors.
 
 
 
• **Global Recognition:**
 
 
• NSE is ranked among the **largest exchanges globally** in terms of trading volume.
 
• It has received multiple awards for its role in modernizing India’s capital markets and promoting financial inclusion.

questions.question: What was the growth target for twelfth five year plan in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 3**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Twelfth Five-Year Plan** in India covered the period from **2012 to 2017**. 
• The growth target for the Twelfth Five-Year Plan was set at **8%** annual average growth in the Gross Domestic Product (GDP). 
• It aimed to achieve **sustainable and inclusive growth**, with a focus on reducing poverty and regional inequalities. 
• The plan emphasized investments in **health, education, infrastructure, and agriculture** to enhance overall development. 
• The target was considered ambitious, given the challenges such as a slowing global economy and domestic constraints like inflation and fiscal deficits. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Five-Year Plans in India:** 
• The concept of Five-Year Plans was introduced by **Jawaharlal Nehru** in **1951**, inspired by the Soviet model of planned economic development. 
• The **Planning Commission** was responsible for formulating and monitoring these plans until its replacement by the **NITI Aayog** in **2015**. 
• The primary objective of Five-Year Plans was to promote **economic growth, self-reliance, and social equity**. 
• **Key Features of the Twelfth Five-Year Plan:** 
• It focused on achieving **inclusive growth** by ensuring benefits reach marginalized sections of society. 
• Emphasis was placed on improving **infrastructure**, including roads, railways, power, and irrigation. 
• It aimed to reduce the **poverty rate** by creating employment opportunities and enhancing social welfare schemes. 
• Environmental sustainability was highlighted, with policies to address **climate change and resource management**. 
• **Challenges Faced During the Twelfth Plan Period:** 
• Global economic slowdown affected export growth and investment inflows. 
• High levels of **inflation** and **fiscal deficits** posed macroeconomic challenges. 
• Structural bottlenecks in sectors like **agriculture and manufacturing** hindered progress. 
• Implementation issues with various programs affected the achievement of targets. 
• **Achievements of the Twelfth Five-Year Plan:** 
• Progress was made in **poverty reduction**, with millions lifted above the poverty line. 
• Significant improvements in **healthcare and education** indicators were achieved. 
• Infrastructure development witnessed growth, especially in **renewable energy** and transportation. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Planning Commission vs. NITI Aayog:** 
• The **Planning Commission** was established in **1950** to formulate Five-Year Plans. 
• In **2015**, it was replaced by the **NITI Aayog**, which serves as a policy think tank focusing on **cooperative federalism**. 
• NITI Aayog emphasizes **bottom-up planning**, involving states in decision-making processes. 
• **Growth Targets in India:** 
• Growth targets are set to achieve desired levels of economic development and social equity. 
• These targets are influenced by factors like resource availability, population growth, and global economic conditions. </ul

questions.question: As per September 2024, according to the Ministry of External Affairs in India, there are ______ million Indians residing abroad who are either NRIs or OCIs.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**32 million**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• As per the data released by the **Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), India**, in **September 2024**, the estimated number of **Indians residing abroad**, including **Non-Resident Indians (NRIs)** and **Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs)**, is approximately **32 million**.

• This includes Indians living in countries across continents such as the **United States, the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia**, and other nations.

• The figure represents a mix of Indians who have either migrated for work, education, or permanent settlement and those who maintain Indian citizenship but reside abroad temporarily.

• The MEA consistently updates this figure through consultations with embassies, consulates, and official surveys conducted worldwide.

• These individuals contribute significantly to India’s **economy** through **remittances**, which stood at a record high of **$111 billion in 2023**, making India the world’s largest recipient of remittances.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Non-Resident Indians (NRIs):**

• An **NRI** is an Indian citizen who resides outside India for employment, education, or other purposes for an indefinite period.

• NRIs retain their Indian citizenship but are typically subject to specific tax regulations under the **Income Tax Act, 1961**.

• They contribute significantly to the Indian economy through **foreign direct investments (FDIs)** and remittances.

• **Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs):**

• OCIs are individuals of Indian origin who hold citizenship in another country but are granted certain privileges in India, such as **visa-free travel** and the ability to own property.

• The **OCI card** was introduced under the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2005, to strengthen ties between India and its diaspora.

• OCIs are not allowed to vote or hold constitutional office in India.

• **Indian Diaspora:**

• The Indian diaspora is the **largest in the world**, with members spread across **more than 200 countries**.

• Key regions of settlement include the **Middle East** (especially GCC countries), **North America, Europe, and Southeast Asia**.

• They are known for their contributions to local economies and their role in enhancing **India’s soft power** globally.

• **Remittances to India:**

• India received a record **$111 billion** in remittances in **2023**, accounting for approximately **3% of its GDP**.

• The major sources of remittances include the **United States, UAE, Saudi Arabia, and the UK**.

• This financial inflow helps India maintain a stable **current account balance** and supports rural households significantly.

• **MEA Initiatives for Indians Abroad:**

• The **Pravasi Bharatiya Divas**, celebrated annually, recognizes the contributions of the Indian diaspora to India’s development.

• The **e-Migrate system** ensures the safety and welfare of Indian workers migrating to other countries for employment.

• The **Vande Bharat Mission** was launched to repatriate Indians stranded abroad during the COVID-19 pandemic.

questions.question: In which cell is the respiratory pigment haemoglobin found in humans?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Red blood cells**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Haemoglobin** is a respiratory pigment found exclusively in **red blood cells** (RBCs) in humans. It is responsible for transporting oxygen from the lungs to tissues and carrying carbon dioxide from tissues to the lungs. 
• **Red blood cells** are specialized cells that lack a nucleus in their mature form, allowing more space for haemoglobin molecules. 
• Haemoglobin is a **protein** containing iron that binds to oxygen, forming oxyhaemoglobin, which is transported to various parts of the body. 
• RBCs are produced in the **bone marrow** and have a lifespan of approximately **120 days** before being broken down in the liver and spleen. 
• The presence of haemoglobin gives RBCs their distinctive **red color** and plays a vital role in maintaining the body’s oxygen supply. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
• **Blood Platelets:** 
• Platelets, also known as **thrombocytes**, are small cell fragments involved in blood clotting. 
• They do not contain haemoglobin and their primary function is to prevent excessive bleeding by forming clots at injury sites. 
• Platelets are produced in the **bone marrow** and have a lifespan of **7-10 days**. 
• They play a critical role in wound healing and maintaining vascular integrity. 
• **Monocytes:** 
• Monocytes are a type of **white blood cell (WBC)** involved in immune responses. 
• They do not contain haemoglobin but are responsible for **phagocytosis**, where they engulf and destroy pathogens and cellular debris. 
• Monocytes differentiate into **macrophages** and **dendritic cells** once they migrate to tissues. 
• They are key players in both innate and adaptive immunity. 
• **Nerve Cells:** 
• Nerve cells, or **neurons**, are specialized cells responsible for transmitting electrical signals throughout the body. 
• Unlike RBCs, they do not contain haemoglobin and are not involved in oxygen transport. 
• Neurons consist of three main parts: the **cell body**, **axon**, and **dendrites**. 
• They play a vital role in coordinating bodily functions and processing sensory information. 
• **Important Points:** 
• **Haemoglobin** is composed of four protein chains and iron molecules, essential for binding oxygen. 
• It facilitates the transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide, ensuring proper cellular respiration and energy production. 
• A deficiency of haemoglobin leads to **anemia**, characterized by fatigue, weakness, and shortness of breath. 
• RBC production is regulated by the hormone **erythropoietin**, secreted by the kidneys in response to low oxygen levels.

questions.question: How do plants convey information about a touch from one cell to another?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By using electrical-chemical signals**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• Plants do not have specialized nerve tissues like animals. Instead, they rely on **electrical-chemical signals** to convey information between cells. 
• When a plant experiences touch, such as from an insect landing or wind blowing, it generates **electrical signals**, also called action potentials, that travel between the cells. 
• The movement of ions such as **calcium (Ca²⁺)** and other secondary messengers plays a key role in transmitting these signals. 
• These signals can trigger changes in cellular activities, such as the closing of stomata, the release of defensive chemicals, or the rapid movement of plant parts (e.g., the folding of leaves in the sensitive plant *Mimosa pudica*). 
• This process does not involve sound waves, color changes, or nerve tissues, which are mechanisms associated with animals or other systems. **Hence, the correct option is "By using electrical-chemical signals."** 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Electrical Signaling in Plants:** 
• Plants use electrical signals, such as **action potentials** and **variation potentials**, to communicate within and between cells. 
• These signals are typically triggered by external stimuli like touch, wounding, or changes in light and temperature. 
• For example, the Venus flytrap uses electrical signals to snap shut its leaves when prey touches its sensory hairs. 
• **Role of Calcium Ions (Ca²⁺):** 
• Calcium ions act as **secondary messengers** in plant cells, helping to relay signals from the site of touch or damage to other parts of the plant. 
• Changes in calcium concentration within cells help activate specific genes or pathways for defense or adaptation. 
• **Plant Movement Responses:** 
• Touch-sensitive plants like **Mimosa pudica** exhibit rapid leaf movements in response to touch, a phenomenon known as **thigmonasty**. 
• Other movements, like phototropism (growth towards light) or gravitropism (growth in response to gravity), are slower but also involve chemical and electrical signaling. 
• **Misconceptions About Plant Communication:** 
• Plants do not have nerve tissues or produce sound waves for communication, unlike animals. 
• Color changes in plants, such as leaves turning yellow or red, are usually due to environmental factors or physiological changes, not a means of communication. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Thigmomorphogenesis:** 
• This is a long-term response in plants to mechanical stimulation, such as repeated touch or wind. 
• Plants that experience frequent mechanical stimuli often grow shorter and sturdier to withstand such forces. 
• **Defensive Responses:** 
• Plants can release volatile organic compounds (VOCs) as a chemical signal to warn neighboring plants of herbivorous attacks. 
• Touch can also stimulate the production of **defensive chemicals**, such as toxins or enzymes that deter herbivores. </ul

questions.question: "Taxila", the famous centre of learning, was the capital of which Mahajanapada in ancient India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gandhara**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Taxila**, an important center of learning in ancient India, was the capital of the Mahajanapada called **Gandhara**. 
• The **Gandhara Mahajanapada** was located in the northwestern region of the Indian subcontinent, covering parts of modern-day **Pakistan and Afghanistan**. 
• Taxila was renowned for its world-class **educational institutions**, attracting scholars and students from across the world, including notable figures like **Chanakya, Panini, and Jivaka**. 
• The city's strategic location on ancient trade routes, such as the **Uttarapatha**, made it a cultural and commercial hub. 
• Taxila flourished particularly during the **6th century BCE** to the **5th century CE**, under the influence of various dynasties, including the Achaemenids, Mauryas, Indo-Greeks, and Kushans. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Gandhara Civilization:** 
• The Gandhara region was an important cultural and political hub in ancient India, known for its **Gandhara art**, which combined Indian and Greek artistic influences. 
• The **Gandhara School of Art** is best known for its depictions of **Buddha** in human form, influenced by Hellenistic styles. 
• It was also a center for the spread of **Buddhism**, with numerous monasteries and stupas built during the reign of the Mauryan emperor **Ashoka**. 
• **Taxila University:** 
• Taxila housed one of the earliest known universities in the world, offering education in a wide range of subjects, including **medicine, law, politics, warfare, mathematics, and philosophy**. 
• It was unique in that it did not have a formal admission system; students came to study under specific teachers based on their expertise. 
• **Other Mahajanapadas:** 
• **Avanti:** Located in modern-day Madhya Pradesh, its capital was Ujjayini (modern Ujjain). 
• **Kamboja:** Situated in present-day regions of northern Afghanistan and parts of Central Asia, Kamboja was known for its warrior class. 
• **Kosala:** Located in modern-day Uttar Pradesh, its capital was Ayodhya, and it played a significant role in the early history of Buddhism and Jainism. 
• **Taxila’s Decline:** 
• Taxila's prominence declined after the invasions of the **Huns** in the 5th century CE, which led to the destruction of the city and its institutions. 
• The region subsequently lost its significance as a center of learning and cultural exchange. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Panini:** The ancient grammarian who authored **Ashtadhyayi**, the foundational text of Sanskrit grammar, was associated with Taxila. 
• **Chanakya:** Also known as **Kautilya** or **Vishnugupta**, the advisor to Chandragupta Maurya and author of the **Arthashastra**, is believed to have studied and taught in Taxila. 
• **Jivaka:** A renowned physician during Buddha's time, who studied at Taxila, is considered one of the earliest surgeons in history. 
• **UNESCO World Heritage Site:** The ruins of Taxila were declared a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in 1980, recognizing its historical and cultural significance. 
• **Archaeological Discoveries:** Excavations in Taxila have unearthed numerous artifacts, including stupas, coins, and sculptures, shedding light on its rich cultural heritage.
